_description: Architectural decision records: routing, state management, build pipeline, major library choices, cross-cutting refactors. Append only; supersede with a new entry instead of editing.

title: No REST API — Inertia.js with server-rendered React
context: Single-user local app; a separate JSON API plus a client fetch layer would add ceremony with no payoff.
decision: Controllers return Inertia::render() for GET and redirect()->back() for mutations; React pages receive typed props directly. No JSON API.
rationale: Removes the API/client contract and serialization boundary; one source of truth for props; simpler to keep TypeScript types aligned.
consequences_positive: Less code
No API versioning
Typed props end-to-end
consequences_negative: No external/programmatic API surface
Coupled to Inertia

title: Soft deletes plus toast-level undo for user data
context: An assistant once deleted real financial data; deletions must be recoverable.
decision: Core tables (assets, categories, goals, pension) use SoftDeletes; destroy controllers flash an undo URL that a restore endpoint consumes.
rationale: Recoverability for a personal-finance app without a full trash UI, which the user judged unnecessary.
consequences_positive: Accidental deletes recoverable
Cheap to build on existing routes
consequences_negative: No UI yet to browse/restore older soft-deleted records

title: Broker sync reuses bank_synced_at; connection-type-agnostic model deferred
context: Scalable Capital balances (a broker, not a bank) are synced into assets via the same value-sync path as open-banking accounts. The Scalable sync stamps assets.bank_synced_at and the UI badge keys off (bank_synced_at set AND NOT bank_linked) to mean 'broker-synced'. The 'bank_' naming now describes more than banks.
decision: For the stopgap Scalable integration, reuse the existing bank_synced_at column and the bank_linked-derived signal rather than introducing a new sync-source abstraction. A future refactor should introduce a connection-type-agnostic model (e.g. a generic synced_at / sync_source on assets, or a polymorphic 'data source' link table) so bank, broker, and future sources are first-class.
rationale: The integration was an early stopgap; a schema/abstraction refactor would be wasted effort before the source stabilised. Reusing bank_synced_at kept the change small and let the existing freshness UI work unchanged.
consequences_positive: Minimal change
Existing freshness UI reused
No migration churn for a stopgap
consequences_negative: Column/flag names (bank_synced_at, bank_linked) no longer match reality once a broker writes them
Badge logic relies on the implicit 'synced but not bank_linked' convention
Cash asset is anchored only by name+category (fragile to rename), unlike ISIN-anchored holdings

title: In-app Scalable CLI login runs as a queued job with cache-backed status polling
context: The official Scalable CLI login (sc login) is a device-code flow: human_only, no JSON output, and it blocks while polling for the user's browser 2FA confirmation. Surfacing that flow in the Settings UI can't be done in a normal HTTP request — a blocking child would freeze the single-threaded dev server, and the activation URL must reach the UI in real time.
decision: Login runs in a queued job (RunScalableCliLogin, tries=1, timeout=900) in the existing queue:listen worker. The job runs `sc login` via Process::start, parses the activation URL + user code from plaintext stdout with a tolerant regex, and publishes them through ScalableLoginState (a cache wrapper at key scalable.login, ~20min TTL). The Settings card polls GET /scalable/cli/login/status (plain JSON, not Inertia) every 2s and shows the clickable URL + copyable code + spinner. Success is confirmed by `sc whoami --json` after exit 0 — the login's own text is never trusted. Card health uses a live whoami (cli_logged_in).
rationale: The worker is a blocking context by design, so it absorbs sc login's blocking without stalling requests. Cache (database driver, shared with the worker) holds the ephemeral URL/code with TTL so a crashed worker self-clears. Plaintext parsing is the only fragile part (mitigated by the pinned CLI version, a tolerant regex, raw-output logging, and the authoritative whoami gate). The terminal fallback (docker exec sc login) always remains.
consequences_positive: No request ever blocks on sc login
Real-time URL/code in the UI via lightweight JSON polling
Success always verified by whoami, never by login text
Crashed-worker pending self-expires via cache TTL + isInProgress staleness check
consequences_negative: Activation URL is parsed from human_only plaintext stdout — a CLI reword would leave it uncaptured (recoverable via retry/terminal)
Adds a cache-backed transient state separate from scalable_connections
queue:listen processes one job at a time, so a hung login occupies the worker until its 900s timeout

title: Connection-agnostic sync columns: synced_at + sync_source replace bank_synced_at
context: adr_20260603_214500_7b2c deferred a naming fix: both the bank sync (Enable Banking) and the broker sync (Scalable) stamped assets.bank_synced_at, so the name lied, and the UI badge told bank from broker by exclusion (synced-but-not-bank_linked = broker). With the Scalable CLI now the permanent broker source, the debt was worth paying down.
decision: Renamed assets.bank_synced_at -> synced_at and added assets.sync_source ('bank'|'broker', NULL when never synced; constants Asset::SYNC_SOURCE_BANK/BROKER). FetchBankBalances stamps sync_source='bank', FetchScalableBalance stamps 'broker'. A single migration renames, adds the column, and backfills existing rows by the same active-link logic the app used (inlined, not via BankAccount::activeLinkKeys(), for migration-safety). The AssetTable/AssetForm badges now read sync_source explicitly instead of the exclusion heuristic. bank_linked stays (still derived in FetchAssetsByMonth) because it means 'an active connection manages this row NOW' (edit-lock/delete-warning) — a different signal from 'who last synced'. DisconnectController now clears both synced_at and sync_source.
rationale: Honest, explicit columns: the badge no longer guesses, and the schema no longer claims 'bank' for broker-synced rows. Keeping bank_linked separate preserves the live-link semantics the edit-lock needs.
consequences_positive: Column names match reality
Badge reads source explicitly, no exclusion guess
Future sync sources are first-class via sync_source
Disconnect fully clears sync state
consequences_negative: Cash asset is still anchored by name+category (unchanged by this work)

title: Adopt Prism for the AI advisor's model transport and tool-calling
context: The advisor talked to Ollama via a hand-written HTTP loop (OllamaAdvisorProvider) and was to gain a cloud Claude driver later; adding tool-calling meant writing a multi-step tool loop for each backend. The requirement is that local (Ollama) and cloud (Anthropic) are peers the user chooses at runtime.
decision: Introduce prism-php/prism (v0.100) as the LLM transport behind a single PrismAdvisorProvider implementing AdvisorProvider. The provider picks Provider::Ollama or Provider::Anthropic from services.advisor.driver; the tool-calling loop, message abstraction and streaming are Prism's. Advisor tools are defined once in App\Advisor\Tools\AdvisorToolFactory (model-agnostic) and work with either backend. OllamaAdvisorProvider removed.
rationale: One tool definition + one loop serves both backends instead of two hand-written loops. Empirically validated: a spike showed qwen3:8b via Prism does clean tool round-trips with the <think> block stripped, and streaming works alongside tools. Prism pulls no per-provider SDKs (built on Laravel's HTTP client), keeping the dependency light in an otherwise minimal composer.json.
consequences_positive: Adding a provider is a config change, not a new loop; streaming + tool events unified; structured output available for free later.
consequences_negative: Prism is 0.x so the API can break between minors (pin the version); on Ollama only ToolChoice::Auto is available (fine for an advisor); the app now carries its first heavy dependency.

title: Advisor generative UI via widget-emitting tools (not the Vercel AI SDK)
context: The advisor chat rendered every reply as markdown text. We wanted the model to CHOOSE to render rich, sometimes interactive components (starting with an interactive PAC simulator) instead of prose, without the app forcing it. A model outputs text, not React, so 'the model picks a component' must reduce to: the model emits a structured signal and the frontend maps it to a prebuilt component.
decision: Each advisor tool that has a UI counterpart, besides returning the annotated text the model reasons over, calls AdvisorWidgetCollector::add(type, data) with app-computed (deterministic) data. The collector is a request-scoped singleton (twin of AdvisorToolActivityReporter), armed by ContinueChat::complete on the pending assistant message; accumulated widgets are persisted to a new advisor_messages.widgets JSON column. All three message serializers (Index/Status/Message controllers) emit widgets. Frontend: Message.widgets union type, AdvisorWidgets dispatcher (switch on type), MessageBubble renders widgets UNDER the prose. First widget: pac_simulator, whose compound projection is mirrored in lib/pacMath.ts so sliders recompute live with no model round-trip.
rationale: The model chooses the component by choosing the tool it ALREADY calls; the numbers come from PHP (BuildAdvisorContext), so a weak local model cannot inject wrong figures into the UI (the recurring sign-flip footgun). Rejected the Vercel AI SDK generative-UI framework: same pattern, but it is a Node/JS SDK tied to streamText/streamUI in a Next.js route, whereas the advisor is Laravel+Prism (PHP) with a background-job+polling model (streaming froze the server) and 3 drivers already in PHP — adopting it means rewriting the whole advisor layer in Node for zero gain.
consequences_positive: One mechanism reuses the existing tool-loop and the activity-reporter pattern; works on all 3 drivers (Ollama/Regolo/Anthropic) because it is just a tool call; model cannot break widget shape; interactive widgets recompute client-side.
consequences_negative: The PAC compound formula is duplicated PHP<->TS (kept in step by tests on both sides); adding a widget touches ~6 files (tool, type union, component, dispatcher).

title: Advisor memory is the one profile field written autonomously (no confirmation card)
context: The advisor follows an 'AI proposes, user applies' boundary: every profile change (name, horizon, risk tolerance, income, emergency fund, birth date, risk-notes) is emitted as a one-click confirmation card (profile_proposal widget, POST /advisor/profile) and never written silently. The durable-memory field (preferences/facts to remember, e.g. 'non vuole obbligazioni') originally rode the same cards via a `memory` param on propose_profile_update / confirm_profile_fact. The user found the per-fact card friction annoying for what is a low-stakes note, and asked that memory be kept up to date by the AI on its own, told after the fact.
decision: Memory is the SINGLE profile field the advisor updates autonomously. A dedicated tool remember_fact(fact) writes it immediately (append-merge via mergedMemory: bulleted, de-duplicated, clamped to the column limit) and returns text instructing the model to tell the user what it stored. The `memory` param was removed from propose_profile_update and confirm_profile_fact, so memory no longer routes through any card. All other profile fields keep the confirmation-card flow unchanged.
rationale: Memory is additive, low-stakes, and never overwrites prior facts, so a confirmation gate added friction without protecting anything — unlike horizon/risk/income where a wrong value skews the whole analysis. Writing autonomously and reporting back ('Ho memorizzato che...') matches how the user wanted it to feel. remember_fact reuses the isProfileFactAllowed gate so it only writes during a real chat turn (no-op on report generation / unit tests where no assistant message is armed), keeping the write side-effect scoped.
consequences_positive: No card friction for durable preferences; the advisor keeps memory current mid-conversation.
The AI-proposes-user-applies boundary stays intact for every consequential field.
Append-merge (mergedMemory) still guarantees earlier facts survive and duplicates are skipped.
consequences_negative: One profile field now writes without explicit user confirmation; mitigated by it being additive-only and always reported back in the reply.
The model must be steered (both chat prompts) to route durable facts to remember_fact and everything else to the cards; a confused model could mis-route.

title: Investor profile lives on the Goal page; the horizon is derived from the goal's target date
context: The investor profile (name, birth date, horizon, risk tolerance, notes, memory) was only reachable through a 'Profilo' button inside the AI advisor page, while the Goal (target value, target date, allocation, milestones) had its own nav section. The two describe one thing — who the user is and where they are heading — but sat far apart, and two fields overlapped: InvestorProfile.horizon (short/medium/long, hand-picked) and Goal.target_date said the same thing with no synchronisation, so a profile could claim 'breve' beside a 2040 goal. Both statements were rendered into the SAME advisor prompt (RenderAdvisorContext::profileSection + the goal briefing), leaving the model to guess which to believe. ContinueChat's interview slots already treated target date and horizon as one concept ('date' slot matches both a year and 'entro N anni'), so the unification was half-present.
decision: The Goal page owns the profile: FetchGoalData exposes a `profile` prop, Components/Goal/ProfileCard renders it above the goal progress (and above the empty state when no goal exists), and editing opens the existing Advisor/ProfileDialog so there is one form and one write path (POST /advisor/profile). The advisor's 'Profilo' button became 'Profilo e obiettivo' linking to /goal; the now-dead ProfileDialog mount and the never-used ProfileSummary were deleted. The horizon became derived: Goal::horizon() buckets the years to target_date (<3 short, 3-10 medium, 10+ long, null without a date, 'short' once elapsed). It was removed from InvestorProfile::$fillable, from StoreInvestorProfileRequest, and as a parameter of propose_profile_update / confirm_profile_fact; both tool descriptions now steer the model to propose_goal_core instead. The DB column stays (holding the last hand-entered value) but nothing reads it. ProfileProposal filters its POST through a WRITABLE_FIELDS allowlist so sessions persisted before the change cannot resend a stale horizon.
rationale: Risk tolerance was NOT unified: it has an independent meaning (tolerance for a drawdown) and a real consumer — AdvisorToolFactory::expectedAnnualReturn maps low/medium/high to 3/5/7% real return, which compounds across the whole projection. Horizon had no such consumer: it only ever reached a line of prompt text, while target_date carried the same fact to the day. Deriving it removes a contradiction from the advisor prompt (the feature with the most invested work) and one hand-maintained field, without touching the field that does real work.
consequences_positive: One source of truth for the horizon; the prompt can no longer contradict itself, and the rendered line says where the value comes from.
Profile and goal are visually and conceptually adjacent; one edit surface instead of two.
One less field to keep in sync by hand; moving the goal date updates the horizon everywhere.
The stale-horizon path from old sessions is covered by a test, not just by the server ignoring the field.
consequences_negative: The horizon can no longer be stated independently of a goal: with no goal (or no target date) it reads '—' and the advisor is told nothing.
The legacy investor_profile.horizon column lingers as dead data; a reader going straight to the DB could mistake it for live.
Goal::horizon() duplicates the bucket thresholds that the UI labels also spell out (ProfileCard / ProfileDialog HORIZON_RANGES).

title: Cashflow pages by month server-side; whole-history aggregates move to server props
context: Cashflow\IndexController shipped the entire bank_transactions table on every visit to /cashflow, and the page grouped the rows by day filtering them in memory with two date inputs. The payload grew with every sync and the day-grouped list was unbounded. The emergency-fund coverage and the two 'media / mese' cards were computed client-side over that full array.
decision: The page shows one month at a time, selected with a ?month=YYYY-MM-01 query param and a prev/select/next control, reusing the convention InputData (Bilancio) already established: a FormRequest with a defaulting month() accessor, an Action returning the whole prop array, and an Inertia visit. Cashflow deviates on the visit itself: it uses a partial reload (only: ['transactions', 'month'], preserveState + preserveScroll) instead of Bilancio's full preserveState: false visit, because the page holds staged edits and filters that must survive a month change, and the other props are month-independent. Future months are unreachable: the next arrow is disabled at the current month, the select lists only past months, and the FormRequest clamps a hand-typed future month to the current one. Prop building moved out of the controller into App\Actions\Cashflow\FetchCashflowData. The date-range inputs were removed; the month selector is the only period control. The whole-history figures now come from props, computed by the pre-existing ComputeMonthlyExpense and ComputeMonthlySalary actions, plus App\Actions\Transactions\FetchTransactionMonths for the month list.
rationale: A single month is the natural unit for reviewing bank transactions, and the averages cannot be derived from one month's rows — they had to move server-side regardless. Reusing the ?month= pattern kept a second period-navigation idiom out of the codebase.
consequences_positive: Bounded payload and bounded list, independent of history length.
Cashflow's Index controller now follows the controller-delegates-to-Action convention like every other Index page.
The averages and the emergency-fund coverage are stable numbers that no longer shift with a UI filter.
A booking_date index was added: the pre-existing composite index leads with bank_account_id and cannot serve a month range scan.
consequences_negative: The partial reload keeps staged edits alive across months, so a save can post edits belonging to a month that is no longer displayed. Harmless — the PATCH is keyed by transaction id — but the confirmation bar is the only cue that they are still pending.
The emergency-fund coverage no longer reflects unsaved edits — it updates after saving, when the page reloads.
The server-side averages ignore rows with a NULL flow_type (never classified), where the old client-side calculation counted them as expenses.

title: The Investments section is absorbed into Bilancio, renamed 'Bilancio investimenti'
context: /investments was a page consuming a single prop (ComputePositionReturns' output) that rendered an aggregate summary, a positions table and a CSV-export button. Its per-position detail was already reachable from Bilancio: AssetTable opens the same TransactionsDialog on any transaction_managed asset. Its aggregate was already rendered by the Dashboard (PortfolioInsights), the Advisor prompt and the Advisor list_positions widget. Its CSV-export button was already duplicated in Settings under Dati -> Import/Export.
decision: The positions table and the aggregate move into /input as Components/Data/PositionsCard.tsx, fed by a new positionReturns prop on FetchInputData. The Investments page, its Analytics\InvestmentsController and the /investments route are deleted. The nav entry is removed and the /input label becomes 'Bilancio investimenti'. The duplicate CSV button is dropped, not moved: the Settings one already covers it.
rationale: The data belongs where the assets are logged; a separate section for one prop's worth of numbers was navigation cost without content. Deleting the duplicated export button removed a second entry point to the same endpoint.
consequences_positive: One fewer nav entry and one fewer page for the same information.
The positions card renders nothing when no asset is transaction-managed, so Bilancio is unchanged for a user with no broker import.
File names and routes stay put (InputData.tsx, /input, input.index, Assets\IndexController), consistent with the documented convention that file names don't track UI titles.
consequences_negative: The positions figures are whole-history and ISIN-deduplicated while every other prop on the page is scoped to the selected month; the card states this explicitly, but it is a mixed-scope page.
The aggregate is now rendered in three places (positions card, Dashboard PortfolioInsights, Advisor) from the same action.
/export/csv keeps only the Settings entry point.

title: The Cashflow page leads with metrics; the transaction list moves behind a dialog
context: /cashflow had grown into a transaction editor wearing a dashboard's clothes: the per-day transaction list occupied most of the page while the figures the page exists for (average salary, average expense, emergency-fund coverage) were four small tiles above it. The list's height also drove a chain of layout failures — a card squeezed to zero height with its rows rendering outside the visible box, patched with a min-h floor. The owner stated the actual purpose: the page is for knowing average expenses, salary and the emergency fund; the transactions are a detail, interesting only for what is derived from them.
decision: Invert the hierarchy. The page shows, in order: three whole-history metric cards (average salary, average expense, and average saving = salary - expense), the emergency fund as the visual headline (coverage in months, shortfall, and months-to-target at the average saving rate), a monthly net bar chart for trend, a compact card for the shown month, and PositionsCard. The transaction list and its filters move into TransactionsReviewDialog, opened by a button that shows the row count and flags staged edits. The staged-edits Map stays on the page, not in the dialog, so closing it doesn't discard work.
rationale: Matching the page's layout to its stated purpose fixes the layout problems at the root rather than with another height floor: with no list competing for height, the flex-1/min-h-0 chain and the min-h floor all disappear and the page simply scrolls like Dashboard and Settings. The average-saving figure is derived from two numbers already shown, so it adds a genuinely useful metric at no data cost.
consequences_positive: The page answers 'how much do I earn, spend, keep, and how is my fund doing' without scrolling. Layout is ordinary flow, no height contention. Review is still one click away and pending edits are visible on the button.
consequences_negative: The monthly trend chart reads saved state only, so it does not reflect staged unsaved edits, while the shown month's totals do — two calculation paths that must stay in agreement (BuildMonthlyFlowSeries mirrors the client's effective() filters, including treating a null flow_type as an expense). Correcting many rows now costs an extra click to open the dialog.

title: The positions card is deleted: its detail and its aggregate were both already reachable
context: PositionsCard (per-position shares, average cost, cost basis, value, P&L, plus an aggregate) had been tried on /investments, then on /input, then on /cashflow, each time looking for a home and never fitting. On /cashflow it was plainly off-topic — that page is about salary, average expenses and the emergency fund — and being tall and content-sized it was what kept the page from holding a full-height layout. Looking for the right page turned up the reason none existed: every figure it showed was already available elsewhere. The per-position detail is rendered in full by TransactionsDialog, opened from any transaction_managed asset in the Bilancio, which already shows shares, average cost, cost basis, current value, unrealised P&L with percentage and realised P&L. The aggregate is rendered by the Dashboard's PortfolioInsights as the 'Rendimento investimenti' insight, and is also in the Advisor prompt and its get_position / list_positions tools. The owner confirmed consulting these numbers rarely, out of curiosity.
decision: Delete PositionsCard.tsx and its test, drop the positionReturns prop and the ComputePositionReturns dependency from FetchCashflowData, and replace CashflowIndexTest's two positionReturns tests with one asserting the prop is absent. ComputePositionReturns stays where it is consumed: FetchDashboardData, and the Advisor via the Dashboard context.
rationale: The placement question had no answer because the premise was wrong: the card was a parallel structure over data that already had a home. Per-asset figures belong on that asset's own row, which is where the dialog already puts them.
consequences_positive: One component and 10 tests less, with no data lost.
/cashflow no longer runs a whole-history, ISIN-deduplicated computation on every page load for a card consulted rarely.
The card was the reason the page needed a min-h floor and could not hold a full-height layout; that constraint is gone.
consequences_negative: The overview — all positions side by side in one table — is gone; the detail is now reached one asset at a time.
The aggregate on the Dashboard is one insight in a rotating carousel, so it is not permanently on screen.

title: Backups move in-app and off-site, encrypted, replacing the host launchd script
context: Backups were a host-side launchd job invoking scripts/backup.sh, which shelled out to `docker run keinos/sqlite3` and wrote into a Proton Drive folder that the desktop client synced. Every durable part of the chain (the schedule, the Docker dependency, the off-site step) lived on the developer's Mac, so hosting the app anywhere else would silently leave it with no backups. This blocked the decision to run the app on a home machine or a VPS. A second gap: a failed or never-running backup only produced a Log::warning, so the absence of backups was undetectable until a restore was needed.
decision: CreateBackup takes the VACUUM INTO snapshot, encrypts it via EncryptBackup (AES-256-CBC + HMAC-SHA256, streamed in 1 MiB chunks), and uploads it to the filesystem disk named by BACKUP_DISK, pruning the remote by the timestamp embedded in the object key. Laravel's scheduler runs `backup:run` at 03:00 and `backup:health` at 09:00; failures and staleness surface as backup_failed / backup_stale notifications that auto-resolve on the next success. `backup:restore` downloads, verifies and decrypts. scripts/backup.sh and the launchd job were removed.
rationale: The app already had every ingredient: VACUUM INTO needed no external sqlite3 binary, the s3 disk was configured with AWS_ENDPOINT (so any S3-compatible provider works), the scheduler ran four commands already, and the persisted notification system existed for exactly this class of event. Moving the chain in-app made hosting portability a property of the code rather than of one machine. Encryption is not optional because the archive is the complete financial history landing on third-party storage; a configured remote disk without a key is a hard error rather than a silent plaintext upload. The retention window reads the key's own timestamp, not object mtime, because re-uploads and provider-side copies rewrite mtime and pruning would never catch up.
consequences_positive: Backups behave identically on any host, so the hosting choice no longer depends on the backup design. Off-site is guaranteed by construction rather than by a desktop sync client. A backup chain that stops now notifies instead of failing silently. Restore is a documented command rather than a manual file copy.
consequences_negative: Proton Drive has no S3 API, so the off-site target had to move to an S3-compatible provider (Cloudflare R2 chosen: free at this data volume, S3-native). BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY becomes a critical secret that must be stored outside the backup destination — losing it makes every archive unrecoverable, and rotating it orphans existing ones. Tests covering VACUUM must commit RefreshDatabase's transaction first, since SQLite refuses to VACUUM inside one.

title: Single-user password auth, no registration or reset flow
context: The app held the complete financial history behind no authentication at all: every route was open, and the users table existed only as the default Laravel migration with no domain table carrying a user_id. That was tolerable while it ran on localhost behind FileVault, but it blocked hosting the app anywhere reachable from a phone — the stated goal. Two scenarios drove the decision: a public URL (a VPS) exposes everything to anyone who finds it, and even on a private Tailscale network a lost phone holds a live session, which the VPN cannot defend against.
decision: Password auth for one account. Every route lives inside a Route::middleware('auth') group so new routes are protected by default, with /banking/callback deliberately outside it. A RequireSetup middleware, ordered before Authenticate via $middleware->priority(), diverts a fresh install to /setup and closes that route server-side once an account exists. Login is throttled at 5 attempts per IP+email. Sessions are encrypted and last 30 days. `php artisan user:password` resets the password and clears every session. No registration, password reset, OAuth or 2FA.
rationale: Deliberately omitted features are the point: for a single account, a reset flow is an extra credential path to attack and OAuth adds a third-party dependency, neither of which reduces risk here — the terminal is a sufficient and safer recovery channel. Protecting by group rather than per-route means forgetting to protect a new route is not possible; only deliberately exempting one is. The bank callback must stay open because the bank redirects without our session, and that failure would surface only against the real bank. RequireSetup must outrank `auth` or a fresh install lands on a login page it cannot get past — caught by a test, not by review. The 30-day session is a deliberate usability tradeoff for a phone-opened app, with password change as the revocation mechanism.
consequences_positive: The hosting decision no longer depends on auth work. A lost or stolen device no longer exposes the data. New routes are protected by default. The setup page cannot be used to mint a second account.
consequences_negative: Every existing feature test needed a signed-in user; done centrally in Tests\TestCase with an $authenticate opt-out rather than 28 edited files. A 30-day session means a stolen unlocked device retains access until the password is changed. No reset flow means a forgotten password requires shell access to the host.

title: Front the self-hosted app with a Tailscale sidecar terminating TLS
context: Self-hosting served the app as plain http on a tailnet IP (BIND_ADDRESS). Reachable, but with no https origin: Enable Banking requires an https consent callback, so every bank connect/renew meant starting a throwaway cloudflared tunnel and rewriting APP_URL, and the session cookie had to run with SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=false.
decision: docker-compose.prod.yml runs a tailscale/tailscale sidecar joining the tailnet as its own node (hostname wealth-tracker), using Tailscale serve to terminate TLS on 443 and proxy to the app on loopback. The app container shares that stack via network_mode: service:tailscale and publishes no host port. Node identity persists in a tailscale-state volume; serve config lives in docker/tailscale/serve.json.
rationale: Tailscale issues a real Let's Encrypt certificate for the .ts.net name at no cost and no public exposure — the name resolves publicly but answers only over the tailnet. That turns https from a workaround into a property of the deployment: the bank redirect is registered once instead of per-session, and the secure cookie stays on. A reverse proxy on the host would have required a domain and certificate management for the same result.
consequences_positive: No tunnel in the bank-consent flow; the redirect is registered once
SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE stays true, matching production defaults
The app publishes no host port, so it is unreachable outside the tailnet
APP_URL has no port and is stable across deploys
consequences_negative: TS_AUTHKEY is now required — the prod stack refuses to start without it
Losing the tailscale-state volume re-registers the node as wealth-tracker-1, silently breaking APP_URL and the registered bank redirect
Consent must be completed from a device connected to the tailnet
scripts/tunnel-prod.sh no longer applies to the default deployment; it is kept, guarded, for http-only setups
Moving to a public domain means unwinding the sidecar and restoring a ports: entry

title: PWA installabile senza vite-plugin-pwa, service worker che non cachea mai i dati
context: L'app viene usata principalmente dal browser mobile. Serviva l'installazione sulla home del telefono (icona, standalone, niente barra URL). L'app serve dati finanziari live ed e raggiungibile solo dal tailnet via sidecar Tailscale.
decision: Manifest, icone e service worker scritti a mano in public/ (manifest.webmanifest, sw.js, offline.html, icons/), registrati da resources/js/app.tsx solo in build di produzione. Il service worker cachea esclusivamente /build/* e /icons/* (nomi content-hashed, quindi immutabili) piu la pagina offline; ogni altra richiesta e network-only, con la offline page come fallback per le sole navigazioni.
rationale: vite-plugin-pwa avrebbe aggiunto una dipendenza (il container ha il footgun ERR_PNPM_UNEXPECTED_STORE) e Workbox spinge verso un precache aggressivo dello shell, che qui e proprio il comportamento da evitare: una pagina Inertia servita dalla cache mostrerebbe un patrimonio non aggiornato. Il service worker a mano e poche decine di righe. Registrarlo solo con import.meta.env.PROD evita che si metta davanti al client HMR in sviluppo.
consequences_positive: Installabile su iOS (manifest + apple-touch-icon) e su Android (il service worker abilita il prompt di installazione). Gli asset hashed vengono dalla cache, quindi l'avvio e piu rapido. Offline la PWA mostra una pagina che indica Tailscale come causa probabile invece dell'errore del browser.
consequences_negative: Il service worker va mantenuto a mano se cambiano i percorsi degli asset. Nessun funzionamento offline reale: senza rete l'app non ha dati da mostrare, per scelta. Il bump di CACHE va fatto a mano quando cambia la strategia.

title: Viste Giorno e Settimana in dashboard: ricampionamento lato server, Giorno con carry-forward su 90 giorni
context: La dashboard aveva due granularita (Snapshot, Mese) esposte come props mom*. Serviva aggiungere Giorno e Settimana. Gli snapshot sono unici per data, ma ci sono giorni senza snapshot: lo snapshot giornaliero viene saltato quando una fonte e stale e lo storico piu vecchio e mensile.
decision: FetchDashboardData espone una mappa periods {day, week, month}, ognuno con le stesse serie (netWorthSeries, stackedBar, growthRates, monthComparison, forecast, macroStackedBar, macroMonthComparison), al posto delle props mom*. Settimana tiene l'ultimo snapshot di ogni settimana ISO (formato 'o-W', anno ISO, cosi la settimana a cavallo di capodanno non si spezza). Giorno produce un punto per ogni giorno di calendario negli ultimi 90 giorni fino all'ultimo snapshot, riportando avanti l'ultimo snapshot noto nei giorni senza misura (copie non salvate via replicate()).
rationale: Se Giorno mostrasse solo i giorni con snapshot sarebbe identico alla vista Snapshot, quindi inutile. Il carry-forward rende l'asse temporale regolare senza inventare cali a zero. La finestra di 90 giorni evita centinaia di punti piatti sullo storico mensile, dove il dettaglio giornaliero non esiste. Una mappa per periodo evita di moltiplicare le props (7 per granularita).
consequences_positive: Aggiungere un'altra granularita e una riga in periodSnapshots() e una voce nel toggle. Le varianti day/week/month condividono gli stessi builder gia testati.
consequences_negative: Nella vista Giorno i giorni riportati avanti mostrano variazione 0% e la variazione si concentra sul giorno della misura successiva. Il payload Inertia della dashboard cresce di circa 90 punti per serie.

title: Tetto di spesa del consulente AI in token, applicato in due punti (middleware + provider)
context: L'advisor non aveva alcun limite: ne di token, ne giornaliero, ne di costo. Con Ollama in locale costa solo CPU, ma la stessa app puntata a un modello cloud ed esposta a internet non ha nulla tra un tool loop impazzito e la fattura. La generazione avviene in un job in coda e il tool loop fa piu chiamate al modello per singola risposta.
decision: App\Advisor\AdvisorBudget: tre tetti configurabili in services.advisor.budget — giornaliero, per sessione, e per singola risposta (passato al modello come max_tokens). Il consumo reale e registrato riga per riga in advisor_token_usage dal provider, usando lo usage che il provider stesso riporta. Il controllo avviene in DUE punti: il middleware advisor.budget rifiuta la richiesta HTTP con 422, e PrismAdvisorProvider::attempt() ricontrolla subito prima di ogni chiamata al modello.
rationale: Il solo controllo nel middleware sarebbe aggirabile dal tempo: tra richiesta accettata ed esecuzione del job passano minuti e piu chiamate. Il solo controllo nel provider lascerebbe l'utente davanti a una bolla 'in attesa' che fallisce dopo, invece di una risposta leggibile subito. Il token e l'unica unita misurabile senza conoscere il listino prezzi del provider. Il controllo nel provider sta DENTRO il retry loop perche anche una risposta vuota costa token.
consequences_positive: Il tetto vale su ogni superficie che raggiunge il modello, compreso il report iniziale e il codice di streaming oggi senza chiamanti. Le righe di consumo sopravvivono alla sessione cancellata (nullOnDelete), quindi il tetto giornaliero non si azzera cancellando una chat — che e un click nella UI.
consequences_negative: AdvisorBudget e un singleton request-scoped armato con la sessione (stesso idioma di AdvisorToolActivityReporter): chi lo risolve separatamente deve vedere la stessa istanza o il tetto per sessione non si applica. Lo streaming registra il consumo solo a StreamEndEvent, quindi un chiamante che abbandona il generatore non paga nulla sul registro.

title: Token di installazione obbligatorio su /setup, scritto su disco e nei log
context: /setup crea l'unico account che possiede tutti i dati finanziari. Era aperto a chiunque lo caricasse per primo: su un'istanza raggiungibile da internet la finestra va dall'avvio del container al momento in cui il proprietario arriva a un browser. Prima che esista un account non c'e' nessuna credenziale da verificare.
decision: App\Auth\SetupToken genera 128 bit esadecimali, li scrive in auth.setup_token_path (default storage/app/setup-token.txt, dentro la data directory montata) con umask 0600 e li logga. SetupRequest li esige come campo 'token'. Il comando setup:token li rilegge (--new li sostituisce) ed e invocato dall'entrypoint di produzione a ogni avvio. Il token e cancellato appena l'account esiste. POST /setup e sotto throttle per IP.
rationale: L'unica cosa verificabile prima che esista un account e il possesso della macchina: chi puo leggere il filesystem dell'host o i log del container e gia la persona legittimata. Generato anche su richiesta (al rendering di /setup) e non solo dall'entrypoint, perche un'istanza avviata con `composer dev` avrebbe altrimenti un /setup non protetto. umask invece di chmod successivo: un chmod lascia il file leggibile da tutti nella finestra tra creazione e cambio modo.
consequences_positive: Un'istanza esposta non e piu appropriabile da chi arriva primo. Le installazioni esistenti non sono toccate: con un account gia presente RequireSetup chiude comunque la rotta.
consequences_negative: Un passaggio in piu al primo avvio, da documentare (README, sezione First run). Il token finisce nei log applicativi per scelta: e il prezzo del percorso 'leggilo da docker compose logs'.

title: Container di produzione non-root: entrypoint root che adotta l'uid del mount e fa gosu
context: Il container di produzione girava interamente come root — server web, queue worker, scheduler — sulla macchina che custodisce tutto lo storico finanziario. L'immagine e scaricata da ghcr, non costruita sull'host, quindi non puo conoscere l'uid dell'host al build time; e la data directory e un bind mount posseduto da un uid dell'host.
decision: docker/prod-entrypoint.sh gira due volte. La prima passata e root e fa solo cio per cui root serve: legge l'uid/gid proprietario della data directory (PUID/PGID lo sovrascrivono), ci sposta l'account appuser con usermod --non-unique, prende possesso di /app/storage, /app/bootstrap/cache e della home, poi fa `exec gosu appuser "$0"`. Tutto il resto — migrate, cache, i tre processi — gira non privilegiato. /app resta di root, quindi il codice e in sola lettura per il processo che serve le richieste. Lo stack di sviluppo resta root di proposito.
rationale: Adottare l'uid del mount e l'unico modo per far scrivere il database su qualsiasi host senza chiedere all'operatore di fare chown dei propri dati, dato che l'immagine e pulled. --non-unique perche un gid dell'host puo coincidere con un gruppo di Debian (gid 100 = users) e groupmod rifiuterebbe, lasciando il container incapace di partire. Lo stack dev bind-monta la working copy in scrittura e non esce da localhost: li l'uid deve essere quello dello sviluppatore.
consequences_positive: Una falla raggiungibile via HTTP non e piu una falla raggiungibile come root. CI ora costruisce l'immagine prod e verifica a runtime che nessun processo artisan giri come root, che i tre processi siano su e che un backup atterri 0600.
consequences_negative: `docker compose exec` NON eredita il drop: atterra come root. Qualsiasi comando che SCRIVE (backup:run, config:clear, sc login, user:password) va eseguito con `-u appuser`, altrimenti lascia file di root che l'app non puo piu riscrivere o eliminare. Il volume scalable-cli si sposta da /root/.config a /home/appuser/.config.

title: Firewall del consulente AI: tre strati, piu' dichiarazione AI emessa dall'app e filtro su tutto cio' che il modello scrive
context: L'advisor vede le posizioni dell'utente per nome con valori e rendimenti, accanto a profilo di rischio, obiettivo e stipendio: quattro dei cinque test ESMA35-43-3861 per la raccomandazione personalizzata erano gia' soddisfatti dall'architettura. Il quinto - l'indicazione su uno strumento specifico - era tenuto fermo da una riga dentro resources/advisor-prompts/*.txt, file gitignorati e sovrascrivibili, e quel prompt diceva al modello 'IL CONSULENTE SEI TU' e di non rimandare a un consulente reale. In Italia la consulenza non autorizzata e' abusivismo.
decision: Tre strati. (1) Prompt riscritti: via la cornice 'sei il consulente', dentro il rinvio esplicito all'albo OCF. (2) App\Advisor\AdvisorBoundaries::CLAUSES, costante nel sorgente, anteposta da AdvisorPrompt::load() a qualunque prompt risolto - unico punto di passaggio, due call site. (3) App\Advisor\AdvisorOutputFilter: rimozione per co-occorrenza di direttiva operativa + riferimento a strumento specifico (nomi/ticker/ISIN/categorie dell'utente, anche soft-deleted, piu' token ISIN/ticker non posseduti), applicato in scrittura nei quattro percorsi di ContinueChat e in GenerateAdvisorReport, e di nuovo in lettura via AdvisorMessage::displayContent() chiamato dai quattro serializer. Correzioni WEA-13 dopo la revisione indipendente WEA-10: (4) il filtro si applica a TUTTO cio' che il modello scrive, non al solo `content` - AdvisorOutputFilter::filterWidgets()/filterField() filtrano le chiavi scritte dal modello nei widget (MODEL_WRITTEN_KEYS), e le tappe salvate passano dal filtro sia in scrittura (StoreGoalMilestonesController) sia in lettura (FetchGoalData), perche' restano sulla pagina Obiettivo fuori dal consulente e senza il suo footer. (5) La regola 'rispondi solo in italiano' si sposta dal file di prompt sovrascrivibile dentro AdvisorBoundaries::CLAUSES. (6) La dichiarazione Art. 50 AI Act e il disclaimer MiFID li emette l'app (resources/js/Components/Advisor/AiDisclosure.tsx), non il modello. (7) Nome, note e memoria del profilo passano da RenderAdvisorContext::userText() come ogni altro valore controllato dall'utente nel briefing.
rationale: Il prompt da solo non e' un controllo: e' sovrascrivibile, non versionato e i modelli derivano su conversazioni lunghe. Spostare i limiti in una costante non rende il sistema a prova di manomissione - chi controlla la macchina puo' sempre modificare il sorgente - ma sposta la soglia da 'file di configurazione che nessuno rivede' a 'commit che qualcuno ha firmato', visibile in git diff e nell'obbligo AGPL di pubblicare il sorgente modificato. Il filtro gira due volte perche' i due punti coprono buchi diversi: solo in scrittura lascerebbe a schermo cio' che era gia' in database o cio' che un percorso futuro dimentica di filtrare; solo in lettura lascerebbe il testo non filtrato in database, che e' la copia che conta se qualcuno chiede cosa ha detto il sistema. Il filtro e' idempotente, quindi il doppio passaggio non costa nulla. Le quattro correzioni hanno la stessa forma: una garanzia non puo' dipendere da chi non e' deterministico. Lo Strato 3 e' un filtro lessicale italiano, quindi la lingua e' portante e non puo' stare in un file di configurazione: un self-hoster che cambia lingua spegne il filtro senza toccarlo. La dichiarazione di legge chiesta al modello compariva 2 volte su 10 col prompt privato, mentre in markup compare prima che il modello produca un token e anche se il modello e' giu' o ignora il prompt. Il briefing e' un messaggio `system` e il prompt dichiara che cio' che sta tra virgolette basse e' dato: un valore concatenato grezzo risulta istruzione per omissione, e `memory` e' scritto da remember_fact - l'unico strumento del profilo che scrive senza conferma - quindi persiste e rientra a ogni turno.
consequences_positive: L'affermazione del README 'non raccomanda mai operazioni specifiche' diventa vera nei fatti. La consulenza generica su classi di attivo resta permessa (ESMA ¶48-50), quindi il prodotto non viene svuotato. Il perimetro e' documentato in docs/ai-advisor-firewall.md per l'esame legale. Misurato, non dichiarato: sulle 50 frasi dell'harness ricostruito da WEA-10, 43 passavano il filtro prima e 0 dopo (l'harness originale della revisione segnava 38/50); i falsi positivi restano 0, con un test di guardia per ogni aggiunta rischiosa.
consequences_negative: Il filtro resta lessicale, non semantico. L'affermazione precedente di questo ADR - 'non intercetta una raccomandazione per perifrasi senza verbo direttivo ne' nome di strumento' - era piu' stretta del buco reale e lusingava il filtro: `Vendi la tua posizione piu' grande` ha il verbo direttivo e nessun nome, e passava. Perifrasi e modi non imperativi ora sono coperti (PERIPHRASIS, PASSIVE_DIRECTIVES, NOMINAL_DIRECTIVES, FOREIGN_DIRECTIVES, KNOWN_INSTRUMENTS, lookback a 3 segmenti con deroga EXPLANATORY). Resta fuori cio' che nessuna lista puo' raggiungere: una raccomandazione portata solo per implicazione, e le lingue non enumerate - le liste straniere sono un paracadute contro la deriva in inglese, non copertura di quelle lingue. Over-blocca per scelta. Le liste vanno estese nel tempo, con un test per aggiunta. ContinueChat::runStreaming() filtra cio' che salva ma non i delta gia' emessi: non va collegata a una route senza prima bufferizzare fino a fine frase.

title: AGPL-3.0-only piu CLA con facolta di sublicenza, non cessione del diritto d'autore
context: Il repo dichiarava `"license": "MIT"` e `"name": "laravel/laravel"` ereditati dallo scheletro: un repo pubblico che rivendicava il nome di un altro pacchetto e una licenza non sua. Serviva una base giuridica per distribuire, mantenendo aperta la possibilita di vendere termini commerciali.
decision: AGPL-3.0-only come licenza in uscita (LICENSE verbatim FSF, nessuna riga anteposta), piu CLA.md che concede al titolare una licenza ampia, non esclusiva, con facolta di sublicenza sotto qualsiasi termine. CONTRIBUTING.md e CONTRIBUTORS.md completano il meccanismo manuale di raccolta.
rationale: `-only` invece di `-or-later` perche il titolare e unico e `or-later` delegherebbe alla FSF il potere di cambiare in futuro i termini sotto cui i clienti commerciali usano il software; rilicenziare sotto una futura v4 resta possibile. Licenza ampia invece di cessione perche l'art. 110 LDA chiede prova scritta e l'art. 120 LDA limita a dieci anni i contratti su opere future: una CLA formulata come cessione in bianco rischia la nullita proprio nella parte utile, e il risultato commerciale e identico. Nessun foro esclusivo in §12: verso un contributore consumatore l'art. 33(2)(u) Codice del Consumo lo presume vessatorio, e toglierlo non costa nulla. Testi prodotti in WEA-5.
consequences_positive: La distribuzione ha una base giuridica; il dual licensing resta possibile; GitHub rileva la licenza con punteggio pieno perche LICENSE e byte-identico al testo FSF.
consequences_negative: La CLA non e stata rivista da un avvocato italiano: restano aperte le domande Q1-Q8 di WEA-5, in particolare la titolarita dei 16 commit firmati con l'email aziendale e la proteggibilita del codice co-firmato da un modello. Finche Q1 non e chiusa, la premessa 'unico titolare' su cui poggia tutto non e dimostrata.

title: FrankenPHP come server di produzione al posto di `php artisan serve`
context: L'immagine di produzione serviva l'app con `php artisan serve`, cioe il server di sviluppo integrato in PHP, documentato da PHP stesso come non destinato alla produzione: nessuna supervisione dei processi, file statici serviti attraverso PHP, concorrenza decisa da PHP_CLI_SERVER_WORKERS.
decision: Immagine base `dunglas/frankenphp:1-php8.4`, server avviato dall'entrypoint con `frankenphp run --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile` in modalita NON worker. Aggiunto `docker/php-production.ini` (display_errors off, expose_php off, opcache con validate_timestamps=0).
rationale: La modalita non-worker boota il framework a ogni richiesta esattamente come php-fpm, quindi nessun rischio di stato condiviso fra richieste come in Octane; il guadagno e avere un vero server davanti (statici serviti e compressi da Caddy, keep-alive, HTTP/2). FrankenPHP invece di php-fpm+nginx perche e un solo binario e un solo processo da supervisionare, dentro un container che gia ne supervisiona tre. Le immagini PHP ufficiali non spediscono alcun php.ini, quindi fino a ora l'app girava con display_errors attivo: su un'app finanziaria uno stack trace nella risposta e una divulgazione.
consequences_positive: Server di produzione reale e documentabile come tale; opcache senza stat() a ogni include perche il codice nell'immagine non cambia mentre il container vive; errori nel log del container e non nella pagina.
consequences_negative: L'immagine base e una build ZTS di PHP (FrankenPHP lo richiede), diversa dalla NTS usata finora; l'ENTRYPOINT dell'immagine va resettato esplicitamente o inghiotte ogni `command:` dei compose. Lo smoke test in .github/workflows/ci.yml cerca ora `frankenphp` invece di `artisan serve`, e il controllo non-root e stato allargato a tutti i processi del container perche il server non e piu un processo artisan.

title: Due compose di produzione: standalone generico e prod con sidecar Tailscale
context: `docker-compose.prod.yml` monta un sidecar Tailscale, usa `network_mode: service:tailscale` e rifiuta di partire senza TS_AUTHKEY. Era pero l'unico compose di produzione, quindi la documentazione 'generica' di self-hosting puntava a uno stack che obbliga chi installa ad avere un tailnet.
decision: Aggiunto `docker-compose.standalone.yml`: solo il servizio app, porta pubblicata su 127.0.0.1, nessun sidecar e nessuna chiave richiesta. `docker-compose.prod.yml` resta la variante Tailscale usata dall'istanza del progetto. `scripts/deploy-release.sh` legge COMPOSE_FILE (default: quello Tailscale) cosi il deploy con rollback funziona con entrambi.
rationale: Un override Compose non puo togliere `network_mode`, e `ports` piu `network_mode: service:` e un errore di validazione, quindi la variante generica non poteva essere un file di override: doveva essere un file completo. La duplicazione del servizio app (circa 40 righe) e il prezzo accettato per non costringere ogni self-hoster a Tailscale. Loopback e non 0.0.0.0 perche l'app contiene l'intera storia finanziaria del proprietario e pubblicarla in chiaro sulla rete locale con la sola login davanti non e un default difendibile.
consequences_positive: Chi installa sceglie l'esposizione invece di ereditarla; la documentazione generica puo puntare a uno stack che non presuppone niente.
consequences_negative: Due definizioni del servizio app che possono divergere. Una modifica a volumi, env o healthcheck va replicata in entrambi i file.

title: The pre-squash release tags v1.0.0-v1.2.0 stay on origin; only v2.0.0 was deleted
context: Before the repository went public it was squashed to a single root commit (b251db5 'chore: initial public commit'). Four tags on origin still pointed into the old history: v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.2.0 and v2.0.0. Together they keep 345 commits of the pre-squash history publicly fetchable (release page, tarball, direct SHA); v1.2.0 is the ancestor-superset of the other three. The WEA-4 audit scanned all 1.926 blobs of those commits for credentials and found 0 matches.
decision: Delete v2.0.0, which marked no real release, and leave v1.0.0, v1.1.0 and v1.2.0 in place. Do not re-point them at the squash root either. The 345 pre-squash commits remain public by choice.
rationale: The squash was a tidiness measure, not a containment one: the old history holds no secrets, so nothing is exposed that needs rotating. The three remaining tags, unlike v2.0.0, mark real releases with a public page, and deleting a tag turns its GitHub release into an untagged draft - a visible gap in the release list for no security gain. Deleting them would not even have hidden the commits promptly: they stay reachable by direct SHA until GitHub Support runs garbage collection.
consequences_positive: The public release list stays complete from v1.0.0 onward. No GitHub Support request, no release pages lost, nothing to rotate.
consequences_negative: Anyone who looks past main at the tags can still fetch the full pre-squash history, so the squash only tidies the default view. A future audit will re-flag these tags as pre-squash refs - that is expected, not a regression; see the playbook pb_20261022_171804_c4d8 for the ancestry test.

title: Il canale numerico dell'advisor applica il test di classe al nome della categoria, e lo applica all'intera allocazione
context: Il firewall (AdvisorOutputFilter) e' lessicale e copre il testo. Accanto gli sta un canale che porta le stesse proposizioni come numeri: `allocation` di propose_goal_milestones e i bucket di propose_goal_composition persistono pesi target per categoria in goal_category_allocations, che la pagina Obiettivo ridisegna come glide path a tempo indefinito. Fino a WEA-19 i tre campi di testo accanto passavano da filterField() e le percentuali non passavano da niente: solo exists:categories,name, numeric 0-100 e la somma a ~100. La stessa proposizione era quindi bloccata come frase e salvata come riga. Le clausole gia' dicono che una categoria chiamata come uno strumento va trattata come strumento specifico, e le categorie le nomina l'utente.
decision: AdvisorOutputFilter::namesInstrument() applica a un nome di categoria nudo lo stesso test che mentionsInstrument() applica dentro un segmento: e' strumento se NON sta in GENERIC_CLASS_NAMES E combacia con una posizione dell'utente, un ticker, un ISIN o KNOWN_INSTRUMENTS. instrumentNames() lo gira su un'allocazione intera. Il verdetto e' sull'insieme, mai sul singolo bucket. In proposta non si emette alcuna card e si istruisce il modello a riproporre per classi; in scrittura si rifiuta tutta la submission PRIMA della delete con cui quelle scritture si aprono; in lettura (FetchGoalData, Advisor/IndexController, allocation_vs_target) si restituisce allocazione vuota.
rationale: I pesi sommano a 100 per contratto: scartare la singola riga lascerebbe un'allocazione che non torna piu' e non lo dice. Il rifiuto precede la delete perche' sia la scrittura delle tappe sia quella della composizione sostituiscono tutto cio' che toccano - rifiutare dopo costerebbe all'utente il piano che aveva gia'. La lettura serve perche' le righe salvate prima del gate sono gia' in database, e allocation_vs_target conta doppio: rilegge il target salvato AL MODELLO, restituendogli la propria proposta rifiutata come fatto acquisito e con la voce dell'app. La composizione e' stata chiusa insieme alle tappe perche' altrimenti il gate sulle tappe sarebbe una deviazione, non un limite.
consequences_positive: Le due meta' del firewall dicono la stessa cosa. Un'allocazione per classi (Azionario 60 / Obbligazioni 30 / Liquidita' 10) continua a funzionare identica: e' il prodotto, ed e' il riparo ESMA35-43-3861 par. 48-50 su cui poggia.
consequences_negative: Falsi positivi reali e accettati: una categoria chiamata come il proprio broker (Fineco, Directa) combacia con KNOWN_INSTRUMENTS e fa rifiutare l'allocazione. Il messaggio nomina cio' che ha rifiutato, cosi' l'utente puo' rinominare il bucket. Resta aperta, e non e' questione di codice, se un'allocazione target PER CLASSI condizionata a profilo e obiettivo sia gia' raccomandazione personalizzata ex art. 4(1)(4) MiFID II / artt. 18-bis-18-ter TUF: il gate e' giusto in entrambi gli scenari, ma se la risposta e' si' va ripensato il glide path per classi, non solo quello per strumenti.
